props.title: Cry Freedom
props.initialSlug: A journalist exposes apartheid's brutal truth

sections.content: **Cry Freedom** (1987) stands as one of cinema's most powerful indictments of South African apartheid, centered on the real-life friendship between black activist Steve Biko (Denzel Washington) and white journalist Donald Woods (Kevin Kline). Director Richard Attenborough, fresh from his triumph with **Gandhi** (1982), brings the same epic scope to this searing political drama. The film's first half masterfully documents Biko's rising influence and tragic death in police custody, while the second half follows Woods' dangerous escape from South Africa to expose the truth. Washington's breakthrough performance as Biko earned him his first Oscar nomination, setting the stage for his legendary career.

sections.content: The film belongs to a crucial wave of 1980s anti-apartheid cinema that includes **A Dry White Season** (1989) with Donald Sutherland and **Bopha!** (1993), Morgan Freeman's directorial debut. These films helped galvanize international opposition to apartheid by bringing South African struggles to global audiences. Like **Mississippi Burning** (1988), they used white protagonists as entry points to explore racial injustice, a controversial but commercially effective approach that sparked important discussions about how to tell stories of oppression. SUBHEAD: Impact and Legacy

Attenborough's approach to political filmmaking influenced later apartheid-themed works like **Invictus** (2009) and **Endgame** (2009). His decision to focus on both Biko's activism and Woods' awakening created a template for films about allies in social justice movements, seen later in works like **The Help** (2011) and **Detroit** (2017). The film's unflinching portrayal of state violence and censorship remains relevant for modern films about authoritarian regimes, from **The Last King of Scotland** (2006) to **The Report** (2019).
